title: A policy incentive shorter than the investment's payback period pays firms to wait it out rather than commit
body:
- The investments such a policy targets span years, not months: capital expenditure, regulatory approvals, workforce training, and supply chain integration each take time to complete.
- Supply chains optimised over decades around a particular configuration create path dependencies that resist rapid reconfiguration.
- Businesses will only commit when the policy is predictable over the payback period, legally durable or structurally difficult to reverse, and protected from near-term repeal by electoral change.
- Without perceived permanence, the rational response is to wait out the policy rather than commit irreversible capital.
- An incentive window shorter than the investment's payback period cannot justify the fixed costs when the policy itself may be reversed by future decision-makers.
- Case: Global auto supply chains optimised over thirty years around international parts flows show the depth of path dependency a two-year tariff window cannot overcome.
conversion: An incentive designed to trigger capital commitment instead rewards waiting, so the structural change it targeted never occurs.
